ORIGINAL ARTICLE

Whole-body MRI Versus [18F]FDG PET/CT in Diagnosing and Monitoring Plasmacytomas A Comparative Study

Nieves Gómez León, MD, PhD,*† Isabel Vicuña-Andrés, MD,‡ Beatriz Aguado-Bueno, MD,‡ Francisco Garrido-Enjamio, MD,* Itxaso Galán-González, MD,§ Valentina Castillo-Morales, MD,∥ Adrián Alegre Amor, MD, PhD,*‡ and Roberto C. Delgado Bolton, MD, PhD¶#

Background/Objectives: Current guidelines recommend [18F]FDG PET/CT as the preferred imaging modality for suspected extramedullary bone plasmacytomas, while whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB-MRI) is indicated for solitary bone plasmacytomas. Despite these recommendations, the available evidence comparing the diagnostic efﬁcacy of both techniques remains limited. The aim of this study was to compare the diagnostic efﬁcacy of WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT in the initial evaluation of plasmacytomas.

Methods: We performed a multicenter, observational, and retrospective analysis of patients diagnosed with plasmacytoma who underwent WB-MRI and/or [18F]FDG PET/CT as part of their diagnostic workup. Lesions identiﬁed were categorized by anatomic location, and concordance between WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/ CT ﬁndings was assessed. The McNemar test and Pearson χ2 test were used to compare detection rates between WB-MRI and [18F] FDG PET/CT.

revealed solitary plasmacytoma in 16 patients, concurrent multiple myeloma (MM) and plasmacytoma in 18 patients, and plasmacytoma in 22 patients with a prior MM history. Out of the 56 plasmacytomas, 40 were osseous and 16 were extramedullary. WB-MRI detected 98.2% of plasmacytomas compared with 83.9% for [18F] FDG PET/CT, with a statistically signiﬁcant difference of OR 9 (95% CI: 1.2–394.5), P = 0.021. Concordance was very high for osseous plasmacytomas but moderate for extramedullary plasmacytomas.

Conclusions: These ﬁndings suggest WB-MRI is an alternative to [18F]FDG PET/CT for detecting plasmacytomas. A comprehensive clinical and radiologic assessment is essential for the optimal evaluation of patients with plasmacytoma.

Key Words: plasmacytoma, multiple myeloma, diagnosis, staging, PET/CT, FDG, MRI, bone, extramedullary

(Clin Nucl Med 2025;50:695–706)

Results: The study included 73 patients (33 men) recruited between 2012 and 2023, age range 30–94 years (mean 63.4 ± 12.2 y). Of these, 56 patients underwent both diagnostic tests. Diagnoses

P lasmacytoma is a mass of clonal plasma cells. It can be found as a solitary plasmacytoma (SP) without or with minimal bone marrow involvement ( < 10% of bone marrow plasma cells) or in the setting of multiple myeloma (MM).1–3 SP is relatively rare, accounting for < 5% of plasma cell dyscrasias and with a cumulative incidence of 0.15/ 100.000.2,4 The average age at diagnosis is 55–60 years and is more common in males than females, with a ratio ranging from 1.2:1 to 2:1.5,6 Regarding location and number of lesions, SP can present either as extramedullary (extraosseous) plasmacytoma (EMP), as solitary bone plasmacytoma (SBP), or as multiple solitary plasmacytomas (MSP).7 Nearly 70% of SP are SBP, with the vertebrae being the most commonly affected bones, followed by the ribs, skull, and pelvic bones. EMP can involve any site or organ, most frequently occurring in the head and neck region (sinuses, nasopharynx, and oropharynx), gastrointestinal tract, and lungs.1,7 Prognosis depends on the risk of progression to MM, occurring in 50% of patients with SBP and 30% of patients with EMP within 10 years of diagnosis.7 SP with no marrow involvement has a risk of progression to MM of about 10% within 3 years. SP with minimal marrow involvement has a risk of progression to MM of 20% to EMP or 60% to SBP within 3 years.8 MSP will occur in about 5% of patients with SP during follow-up.1 DOI: 10.1097/RLU.0000000000005954

Gómez León et al Clinical Nuclear Medicine  Volume 50, Number 8, August 2025

PET/CT is considered a complementary imaging technique to nonconclusive MRI ﬁndings, as it has higher sensitivity but lower speciﬁcity. Reliability of the differentiation between benign tumors and pathologic vertebral compression fractures could be improved if quantitative diffusion measurements were available.28 ADC values are signiﬁ-cantly lower in metastatic disease than in benign fractures29 and DWI could differentiate benign from malignant vertebral body collapse with a sensitivity and speciﬁcity of 95.6% and 90%, respectively.30 MRI is mandatory and the preferred technique in patients with suspicion of spinal cord or nerve root compression to accurately assess the level and extent of the lesions and the degree of epidural space involvement.31 Accordingly, in our study, WB-MRI detected all of these cases in contrast to [18F]FDG PET/ CT (P = 0.0039). In summary, [18F]FDG PET/CT surpasses WB-MRI in detecting extramedullary lesions, particularly in cases involving the face and central nervous system (CNS), such as spinal cord compression. Therefore, the choice between these modalities should be guided by clinical suspicion and their availability at each centre. However, when CNS involvement is suspected, WB-MRI should always be included in the evaluation. Currently, there are no guidelines for the assessment of treatment responses in SP. Caer et al7 suggest that the deﬁnitions that are currently applied nowadays in MM can be used in the setting of SBP, while response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST) criteria can be used for assessing treatment responses in EMP. There is no recommendation by the IMWG on the required frequency of plasmacytomas assessment. It has been proposed that the assessment of plasmacytomas identiﬁed by imaging techniques ([18F]FDG PET/CT and/or MRI), should be done 3 months after the initiation of treatment and subsequently at the physician’s discretion if there is still persistent active disease.9 Albano et al14 stated that [18F]FDG-uptake was found to be correlated to the tumour size of SP: [18F] FDG-avid lesions are generally larger (41.4 mm) vs. [18F] FDG-negative lesions (23.5 mm), and the statistical risk of progression was higher in these [18F]FDG-avid lesions. Regarding the follow-up of plasmacytomas, it is important to consider that some lesions can be differently perceived with different imaging techniques or variously interpreted by different radiologists or nuclear medicine physicians. Ideally, the same reader with the use of the same imaging technique should report the baseline and follow-up assessments for a particular patient to minimize both the inter-technique and the inter-reader variability.10 It is key that the procedure guidelines for [18F]FDG PET/CT are followed to improve harmonization of the procedure and interpretation, to reduce variability in the results and their interpretation between different centers and between different studies acquired and interpreted in the same centers but at different time-points. This is essential both for the daily clinical evaluation of patients as well as for research purposes, to make results comparable.10 Also, prospective randomized studies are warranted to obtain high-quality evidence, as has been the case for lymphoma.32 As expected, the best clinical and radiologic response is observed in solitary plasmacytomas, with the lowest responses in relapsed MM with plasmacytomas, as the latter is correlated with a more advanced phase of the disease. Both [18F]FDG PET/CT and functional MRI techniques are recommended tools for evaluating the disease after therapy, and the choice is usually made based on local

clinical practice, availability, expertise, and current IMWG guidelines.11 The evaluation of minimal residual disease (MRD) and the use of functional imaging techniques such as [18F]FDG PET/CT and MRI play key roles in the assessment of patients with multiple myeloma. Although MRD, evaluated through multiparametric ﬂow cytometry (MFC) or next-generation sequencing (NGS), offers high sensitivity to detect disease at a microscopic level, it has limitations due to the irregular distribution of bone marrow inﬁltration and the possibility of sampling unaffected areas. These limitations can be mitigated by combining MRD with functional imaging techniques such as [18F]FDG PET/CT, which are useful for identifying focal lesions and extramedullary disease33 The 2016 IMWG response criteria deﬁned “imaging plus MRD negative” as patients who have MRD negativity by either MFC or NGS and disappearance of any increased radiopharmaceutical uptake in baseline [18F]FDG PET/CT. “Sustained MRD negative” is deﬁned as MRD negativity in the bone marrow (MFC or NGS) and by imaging, conﬁrmed with assessments at least 1 year apart.34 However, [18F]FDG PET/CT presents challenges, such as the lack of standardized criteria to determine positivity or negativity, which complicates uniform interpretation of the results. The Deauville score (DS) ≥4 has been proposed in some studies as a cutoff value to deﬁne positivity in [18F] FDG PET-MRD, given its association with signiﬁcant prognostic impact. Although [18F]FDG PET/CT plays a complementary role, especially in detecting residual disease not identiﬁed by MRD, its utility appears limited in patients with MRD negativity, where [18F]FDG PET positivity is rare, and the results primarily depend on MRD. Additional studies are needed to optimize the combined use of these techniques, standardize [18F]FDG PET/CT criteria, and explore the beneﬁts of achieving sustained MRD negativity.5 In recent years, the advances include the development and implementation in clinical practice of multimodality systems that combine already established techniques, such as [18F]FDG PET/CT and MRI with DWI.35 Since WB-MRI is the most sensitive method for detecting myeloma lesions and staging the disease, incorporating functional information from DWI and [18F]FDG PET/CT could enhance the evaluation of treatment response. Therefore, whole-body [18F]FDG PET/MRI could serve as a comprehensive examination, combining the most sensitive method for detecting bone marrow involvement with the most established technique for evaluating treatment response.23,35 Another area in development related to MM and SP is the use of radiopharmaceuticals different to [18F]FDG, such as [18F]Fluoro-Choline,3 which allows obtaining complementary information that may improve patient management, as different radiopharmaceuticals can provide metabolic information and characteristics of the tumours regarding different aspects of the tumour as has been seen in other neoplastic entities.36 Also, the combination of the information supplied by PET/CT and MRI with other clinical parameters may allow the development of new biomarkers that could have a prognostic value and help in the clinical management of these patients,36,37 with the aim of improving survival.38 Our study presents several limitations that call for caution in the interpretation of our results. One of the limitations of this study was the number of patients included. We are aware that a deﬁnite conclusion regarding

Clinical Nuclear Medicine  Volume 50, Number 8, August 2025 Whole-body MRI Versus [18F]FDG PET/CT in Plasmacytomas

the role of WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT in the management of plasmacytomas can only be drawn from a study that recruits a large number of patients. However, it is very difﬁcult to enroll a large number of patients due to the very low incidence of EMP. The second major limitation of our study was due to its retrospective nature, in which a referral bias, among other potential biases, cannot be excluded. It is necessary to conduct more multicenter prospective trials to solve these issues.

CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, these ﬁndings suggest that WB-MRI is a viable alternative to [18F]FDG PET/CT for detecting plasmacytomas, particularly in accurately assessing bone involvement and potential spinal cord compression. WB-MRI also proves to be a valuable tool for diagnosing facial plasmacytomas, as well as meningeal, epidural, and pituitary space involvement. In addition, WB-MRI offers the critical advantage of avoiding ionizing radiation, while maintaining high sensitivity for detecting hypercellular areas, especially when DWI is employed.

Gómez León et al Clinical Nuclear Medicine  Volume 50, Number 8, August 2025

The existence of soft-tissue involvement in MM has been known since the very ﬁrst descriptions of the disease. Early autopsy studies showed extra-skeletal involvement in 70% of patients with MM.9 In MM, the reported incidence of EMP at diagnosis ranges from 1.7% to 4.5%, while the rate of SBP ranges from 7% to 34%. At relapse, the incidence of EMP disease increases from 3.4% up to 10% while the frequency of SBP remains similar to that observed at the time of diagnosis.9 Imaging techniques are crucial for detecting plasmacytomas, assessing systemic involvement, and evaluating the response to treatment. Diagnosis also requires histologic conﬁrmation of the suspected plasmacytoma and laboratory tests to exclude or conﬁrm the diagnosis of MM.7 According to the latest recommendations from the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG), Whole-body (WB) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred for suspected SBP, while [18F]FDG positron emission tomography (PET)/ computed tomography (CT) is preferred for suspected EMP. However, [18F]FDG PET/CT can also be used for SBP when WB-MRI is unavailable. WB-MRI has higher sensitivity for detecting bone marrow inﬁltration, whereas [18F]FDG PET/ CT can distinguish between active and inactive lesions.10,11 However, few studies have compared WB-MRI and [18F] FDG PET/CT in the diagnosis of plasmacytomas. The aim of the study was to compare the diagnostic efﬁcacy of WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT in the initial diagnosis and staging of patients with plasmacytoma, as well as in the detection of spinal cord compression in these patients.

MATERIALS AND METHODS

Study Design and Patient Eligibility This is a retrospective, multicenter, observational study focusing on the diagnosis of patients with plasmacytomas at

2 university hospitals. Patients were recruited from the haematology departments of these hospitals between 2010 and 2023. All participants underwent histologic evaluations, including bone marrow aspiration and biopsy of osseous or extramedullary plasmacytomas. The histopathologic diagnoses were made according to the criteria established by the IMWG.8 The clinical inclusion criteria were patients presenting: (a) conﬁrmed diagnosis of plasmacytoma through pathologic examination as the key criterion, considering eligible for the study SP, SBP, EMP, and MSP (as deﬁned above), as well as the diagnosis of plasmacytoma in conjunction with MM (either in the form of a plasmacytoma detected synchronously to a MM or of a plasmacytoma detected in a patient with MM during the MM follow-up or during MM progression); (b) age 18 or above; and (c) a maximum interval of 30 days between [18F]FDG PET/CT and WB-MRI at the time of diagnosis. The histopathologic diagnosis was based on IMWG criteria.8 Exclusion criteria included: (a) life expectancy of < 3 months; and (b) inadequate technical quality of WB-MRI and/or [18F]FDG PET/CT. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 75 patients were included in the study, 2 of them being subsequently excluded because of logistical problems. Finally, 73 patients were included in the study. The ﬂowchart for participant selection is presented in Figure 1.

Ethical Considerations All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of institutional and/or national research committees and the 1964 Helsinki Declaration, including its later amendments or comparable ethical guidelines. The study protocol was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of University Hospital La Princesa on December 16, 2022,

Reference or Criterion Standard Histologic evaluations were performed for all patients, including bone marrow aspiration and biopsies of both osseous and extramedullary plasmacytomas. Histopathologic diagnoses followed the criteria established by the IMWG.8 Histologic evaluations were conducted for all patients, which included bone marrow aspiration and biopsy of both osseous and extramedullary plasmacytomas. The histopathologic diagnoses were based on the criteria established by the IMWG.8

MRI Study Protocol, Interpretation, and Image Analysis WB-MRI was performed according to standard protocols using a General Electric (GE) 1.5-T magnet (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI). The protocol included: (a) fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging (FS-T1WI), fat-suppressed T2-weighted imaging (FS-T2WI), short tau inversion recovery (STIR), and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences as well as the calculation of the apparent diffusion coefﬁcient (ADC); (b) coronal FS-T1WI and STIR sequences from head to ankles, (c) sagittal FS-T1WI and STIR sequences covering the entire spine, and (d) DWI sequences from head to ankles. All WB-MRI scans in our study included DWI. In certain cases of plasmacytomas located in the brain and facial regions, a region-speciﬁc protocol was implemented. The interpretation of WB-MRI images followed the same systematic approach used in signal suppression for each anatomic region. Lesions detected on WB-MRI were deﬁned by alterations in signal intensity and their morphol-ogy in FS-T1WI, FS-T2WI STIR, and DWI.

Image Analysis Systematics Each WB-MRI study was evaluated and reported by a team of 2 expert radiologists from neuroradiology and musculoskeletal sections, both with over 15 years of experience. In cases of discrepancies, an ad hoc consensus was reached. The cases were anonymized and presented in random order, with no access to clinical or histologic data.

[18F]FDG PET/CT Study Protocol and Image Analysis [18F]FDG PET/CT studies were performed using the same PET/CT system, equipped with a 6-row detector CT (Biograph 6 TruePoint; Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany), which has a theoretical spatial resolution of 3–4 mm. The system consists of 4 rows of detectors with LSO crystals and a 6-row detector CT with a dose modulation system based on the topogram (CARE Dose; Siemens Healthcare). Acquisition mode was 3-dimensional, with a coincidence detection window of 4.1 ns. The [18F] FDG PET/CT procedure was performed following international guidelines.10

[18F]FDG PET/CT Interpretation and Image Analysis [18F]FDG PET/CT studies were analyzed by a nuclear medicine physician and a radiologist, both experienced in the ﬁeld, using the same workstation (Syngo software system; Siemens Medical Imaging, Erlangen, Germany). Both readings were done independently, and a post hoc

consensus was reached in case of discrepancies, which were resolved through discussion. Independent reading of the CT component of the [18F]FDG PET/CT was not considered in this study, as interpreting [18F]FDG PET/CT as a whole has been a validated technique for over a decade.10 Standardized uptake value (SUV) and maximum SUV (SUVmax) were calculated in the main lesions. Interpretation and image analysis of [18F]FDG PET/CT was done following international guidelines.2,5,7,10,11 The basis of this system is to compare [18F]FDG uptake in the lesions with [18F]FDG activity in the mediastinum blood pool and in the liver, considering lesions as malignant or active when they present an [18F]FDG uptake higher than the liver [18F]FDG uptake.

Response Evaluation Radiologic response to treatment was assessed using WB-MRI and/or [18F]FDG PET/CT imaging. The criteria used for [18F]FDG PET/CT response evaluation were based on international guidelines,2,5,7,10,11 mainly taking into account the modiﬁed Deauville criteria described by Zamagni et al.5 In summary, complete response is deﬁned by the absence of signiﬁcant [18F]FDG uptake in the lesion comparing to [18F]FDG uptake in the mediastinum blood pool and in the liver of the same patient. The criteria used for WB-MRI response evaluation were based on the IMWG consensus criteria.2 The criteria can be summarized as follows: focal lesions that respond to treatment show a decrease in size and number and a complete or partial decrease in high signal intensity (SI) in FS-T2WI, STIR, or high b-value SI. Other ﬁndings include intratumoral or peritumoral fat within/around focal lesions (“fat dot” or “halo signs”) with an increase in SI in T1WI. Responding shows a decrease in high b-value SI, an increase in SI in T1WI, and a decrease in STIR. Nonresponding lesions or relapses show an increase in size and number. ADC measurements offer the capability to quantify disease throughout the skeleton. Clinical response was evaluated applying the International Myeloma Working Group consensus criteria for response and minimal residual disease assessment in multiple myeloma.2 In summary, these criteria consider clinical and laboratory aspects to deﬁne the following categories: stringent complete response, complete response, very good partial response, partial response, minimal response, stable disease, and progressive disease. However, as deﬁned in the IMWG, there is a notable difference in complete clinical response based on the classiﬁcation. Best response is deﬁned as solitary plasmacytomas with complete response, while the worst response is deﬁned as patients with relapsed MM with plasmacytoma. Radiologic response and clinical response were compared.

Statistical Analysis For the descriptive analysis, qualitative variables were presented as frequency distributions and percentages, while quantitative variables were summarized using the mean and standard deviation. A validity analysis was performed, and the agreement between each diagnostic technique and the criterion standard was calculated using the Kappa coefﬁcient (κ), along with 95% conﬁdence intervals (CI). All statistical tests were 2-tailed, and results were considered statistically signiﬁcant when the P-value was < 0.05. Regarding the presence or absence of MM in the plasmacytoma patients, 20 of the 73 patients did not have a MM (in the subgroup of 56 patients, 16 did not present a MM). With regard to the chronology of the plasmacytoma presentation we differentiated 3 categories: (a) solitary plasmacytomas (SP) without known MM during its follow-up, corresponding to 20 of the 73 patients (or 18 of the 56 patients in the subgroup); (b) simultaneous diagnosis of MM and plasmacytoma (synchronous) in 28 of the 73 patients (18 of the 56 patients in the subgroup); and (c) plasmacytoma diagnosed in patients with a prior history of MM, reaching the diagnosis of plasmacytoma during the course of their disease or during its progression, having undergone a median of 3 prior lines of treatment (range: 1–4 lines). Table 1 also presents the number of patients with bone plasmacytoma (56/73 or 40/56) or with extramedullary plasmacytoma (18/73 or 16/56). The monitoring of all plasmacytomas was done with follow-up WB-MRI (n = 65) and/or follow-up [18F]FDG PET/CT (n = 34). The ﬂowchart for participant selection presents more details of the follow-up (Fig. 1).

WB-MRI Versus [18F]FDG PET/CT for the Diagnosis of Plasmacytoma Of the 56 cases of plasmacytoma, WB-MRI was positive in 55 cases (98%), while [18F]FDG PET/CT was positive in only 49 cases (87.5%). According to the McNemar exact test, the difference between the 2 tests for the detection of plasmacytomas was statistically signiﬁcant, with an OR of 9 (95% CI: 1.2–394.5), P = 0.021. Regarding bone plasmacytomas, the concordance between WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT, according to the McNemar test, was 100% (95% CI: 92.7%–100%), κ = 1; the detection of lesions in the skull, cervical spine, thoracic spine, sternal, pelvis, rib cage, and clavicles (Table 2). [18F]FDG PET/CT detected a plasmacytoma in a lower limb, with a negative WB-MRI. There was discordance between positive WB-MRI and negative [18F]FDG PET/CT in one case for the lumbar spine with compression and superior limb pain.

Figure 2 presents the case of a patient with a plasmacytoma in the pelvis. Concordance was lower for extramedullary involvement, at 87.8% (95% CI: 75.2%–95.4%); κ = 0.6; P < 0001, with 7 cases of positive WB-MRI and negative [18F]FDG PET/CT, and one case of positive [18F]FDG PET/CT and negative WB-MRI. Among the 7 cases with positive WB-MRI and negative [18F]FDG PET/CT, the locations were as follows: nasal (n = 1), meningeal (n = 3) orbital (n = 2), pituitary (n = 1). A stomach plasmacytoma was detected with [18F]FDG PET/CT but not with WB-MRI. Figure 3 shows a nasal plasmacytoma and Figure 4 presents the case of a plasmacytoma in the epidural space.

WB-MRI and [18F] FDG PET/CT for the Assessment of Spinal Cord Compression Spinal cord compression was detected by WB-MRI in 11 of the 56 lesions (19.17%), none of them diagnosed by [18F]FDG PET/CT. Figure 5 presents the case of a plasmacytoma that compressed L5.

Clinical and Radiologic Comparison of Treatment Response Evaluation Clinical response was evaluated according to the response and relapse/progression criteria outlined previ-ously. There was no statistically signiﬁcant difference between clinical and radiologic responses (P-value > χ2 McNemar).

Clinical Results In our study, we did not ﬁnd statistically signiﬁcant differences between clinical response and radiologic response (P-value 0.5637). Among patients with bone plasmacytomas, 56% (40 patients) exhibited a clinical response. In contrast, only 35.71% of patients (26 patients) with extramedullary plasmacytoma showed a clinical response. Due to the limited number of cases, these results are not statistically signiﬁcant. Among patients with MM diagnosed with plasmacytoma, 44% are classiﬁed as IgG, 24% as IgA, 24% as light chains, 4% as non-secretory, and the remaining 4% have unavailable data. The majority of IgA plasmacytomas in MM (55.56%) are extramedullary; however, this ﬁnding is not statistically signiﬁcant (P = 0.059) due to the sample size. In our series, solitary plasmacytomas received radiotherapy in 61.11% of cases, while 38.89% received radiotherapy combined with systemic treatment. Among patients with MM diagnosed with plasmacytoma, 92% were treated with a combination of radiotherapy and systemic treatment, while the remaining 8% received only systemic treatment. In relapsed MM with plasmacytomas, 65.22% received combined treatment, and 34.78% received only systemic treatment. There is a notable difference in complete clinical response based on classiﬁcation. The best response was observed in solitary plasmacytomas, while the worst response occurred in patients with relapsed MM with plasmacytoma. Finally, regarding clinical response according to the type of MM, solitary plasmacytoma demonstrated the best responses (84%), as reported in the literature, followed by

light-chain MM (75%), with these data being statistically signiﬁcant (P = 0.004). In our series, the worst response was observed in IgG MM (34%), followed by IgA (36%). When comparing these data with radiologic responses, the ﬁndings were statistically signiﬁcant (P = 0.016). Again, we observed the best radiologic response in solitary plasmacytomas (82.35%), followed by light-chain MM (75%). Lower radiologic responses were noted, consistent with the clinical responses in IgG MM and IgA MM.

plasmacytomas are available to the best of our knowledge. In our study, we found that WB-MRI detected more plasmacytomas than [18F]FDG PET/CT. The degree of agreement between the 2 methods was very good for identifying bone plasmacytomas but moderately good for extramedullary ones. As expected, WB-MRI was better at detecting spinal cord compression. Currently, international guidelines recommend the use of low-dose CT, MRI, and/or PET/CT, considering any of these techniques valid in the study of MM. The choice of imaging test(s) performed is left to each center, based on availability and the current clinical protocols in place.11 The most important information obtained from whole-body imaging in any patient with SP is the exclusion of additional osteolytic lesions, which would constitute a MM, deﬁned as systemic disease. WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/ CT provide high sensitivity and speciﬁcity to detect focal bone marrow inﬁltration. The diagnostic efﬁcacy of [18F] FDG PET/CT is superior to MRI regarding the assessment of focal lesion viability. In contrast, WB-MRI can better assess diffuse inﬁltration because of its higher sensitivity.11 Although the role of [18F]FDG PET/CT, with proven performance in the evaluation of MM, has been well documented, the literature regarding the use of [18F]FDG PET/CT in SP has only been reported in individuals or in a small number of cases.12–15 Kim et al16 showed that [18F] FDG PET/CT has value for staging and radiotherapy planning in SP and potentially could have a role in response assessment after radiotherapy. MRI remains the preferred imaging modality to detect SBP, especially for those located in the spine. The ability to discern soft tissue involvement and additional marrow abnormalities that could be consistent with MM is a characteristic unique to MRI.2,17 SBP is treated with radiation therapy in the majority of cases, so clear delineation for the delivery of radiation to the lesion with clear delimitation of the margins is essential. Therefore, MRI is an important diagnostic tool in the primary staging of plasmacytoma as well as radiotherapy treatment planning. Few studies in the literature compare MRI and [18F] FDG PET/CT in detecting plasmacytomas. Salaun et al13 compared the value of [18F]FDG PET/CT and spine and pelvis MRI for SP in a series of 24 patients at diagnosis for initial staging and after treatment. The diagnostic accu-racy of MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT in detecting lesions were concordant in 12/20 patients (60%) and discordant for the remaining 8/20 (40%). Finally, in 10/20 patients (50%), [18F]FDG PET/CT detected plasmacytoma lesions in 18 areas that were outside the scope of this research. They found that [18F]FDG PET/CT had a higher diagnostic performance for the initial staging of patients due to its broader scope in evaluating different tissue types, as has been seen in other studies in different tumour types. They also concluded that [18F]FDG PET/CT showed a higher efﬁcacy than spine-MRI and pelvic-MRI for therapeutic assessment. A study conducted by Vicuña et al18 compared WB-MRI with [18F]FDG PET/ CT for the diagnosis of plasmacytoma. They concluded that no signiﬁcant differences were observed between the 2 imaging techniques. However, an important caveat is mentioned regarding the statistical power of their ﬁndings, which was limited by a relatively small sample size (34 SP from 22 patients). Gómez-León et al19 compared WB-MRI with [18F]FDG PET/CT in multiple myeloma patients with comparable results for both techniques.

The results of our current study differ from the previous ﬁndings in the literature. It is noteworthy to emphasize that solely MRI of the pelvis and spine, not of the entire body, was employed in earlier comparative investigations. In our study, SBP comprised 67% of all our SP cases and EMP was located primarily in the head and neck region, similar to other articles.7 Both WB-MRI and [18F]FDG PET/CT demonstrated detection rates exceeding 80%. Despite the high overall detection rates, MRI demonstrated superior performance compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT, particularly in detecting extramedullary lesions. This ﬁnding suggests that WB-MRI was more effective than [18F]FDG PET/CT in identifying plasmacytomas. However, despite differences in the overall detection rates between the 2 modalities, there was excellent agreement in speciﬁc regions for the detection of bone plasmacytomas. The moderate agreement is attributed to the failure of [18F]FDG PET/CT to identify speciﬁc EMP, including 2 located in orbits, one in the nose, three in meningeal or epidural spaces, and one pituitary lesion. The superior soft tissue contrast of the MRI could be an advantage in these locations. The analysis of extramedullary plasmacytomas poses a greater challenge, as imaging tests alone cannot distinguish these lesions from more common malignant tumors like metastases or carcinoma, and con-sequently, histologic conﬁrmation is imperative. In our research, the most frequently associated MM subtype with extramedullary involvement was IgA (40%), followed by Bence-Jones MM (20%) (P = 0.033). There is evidence in the literature of the increased risk that IgA MM has to develop extramedullary plasmacytomas.20,21 Akgun et al21 argued that this might be due to lower CD56 expression causing a loss of cell adhesion. The MRI DWI sequence, which is extremely beneﬁ-cial for identifying malignant lesions, has not been used in prior comparison investigations. Actual WB-MRI protocol recommendations include whole-body DWI.22 WB-MRI with DWI has been used for the staging of myeloma and has demonstrated superiority in detecting bone marrow lesions in MM compared with radiographic skeletal survey, [18F]FDG PET/CT, and conventional MRI.23 This has a substantial impact on treatment planning. In addition, DWI can help in the differentiation of plasmacytomas and metastases. A study conducted by Hwang et al24 in a group of 65 patients with 27 bone plasmacytomas and 38 bone metastases compared conventional MRI to DWI. They concluded that the addition of DWI to conventional MRI improves the capabilities of MRI to discriminate between plasmacytoma and bone metastasis in the extremities. Including DWI sequences in the MRI protocol for soft tissue tumors can facilitate the identiﬁcation of highly cellular tumors, manifested as low signal on ADC maps, and aid in selecting tissue targets for biopsy.25 MRI imaging is the established technique of choice when evaluating vertebral compression fractures, with strong evidence for multiple distinguishing imaging features, which can allow relatively conﬁdent characterization of the benign or malignant nature of a vertebral compression fracture.26 With regard to [18F]FDG PET/CT, malignant fractures are expected to demonstrate different distribution patterns and a higher [18F]FDG-uptake compared with benign fractures.
